promptText: What is the fundamental limitation of a single attention head that multi-head attention is designed to fix?
options: A single head must blend every kind of token relationship into one shared similarity geometry and one softmax distribution per token, preventing it from representing multiple distinct relationship types simultaneously
A single head cannot process more than one token at a time during a forward pass
A single head requires far more learned parameters than several heads combined would need
A single head cannot use the softmax function at all, only multiple heads can
explanation: A lone attention head forces one shared notion of relevance per layer, so syntactic, coreference, and topical relationships all get averaged into the same softmax distribution; multi-head attention lets independent heads specialize in different relationship types instead.

promptText: If d_model = 512 and num_heads = 8, what is d_k for each head, and why is each head given this reduced dimension rather than the full 512?
options: d_k = 64; each head works on a smaller slice so the total parameters and compute across all heads stay roughly equal to one full-size head, instead of multiplying cost by the number of heads
d_k = 512; every head always operates on the full model dimension regardless of head count
d_k = 8; d_k is defined to always equal the number of heads
d_k = 64; heads are shrunk purely to reduce total parameter count below what a single-head model would need
explanation: d_k = d_model / num_heads = 512/8 = 64; splitting the dimension rather than multiplying it is precisely what keeps total Q/K/V parameters and FLOPs roughly constant regardless of head count.

promptText: What does concatenating the per-head outputs in multi-head attention accomplish, and what does it NOT accomplish on its own?
options: Concatenation lays the heads' outputs side by side to restore the full d_model width, but it does not mix or blend information across heads — that mixing happens only via the subsequent W_O projection
Concatenation both restores the model width and fully blends every head's information together
Concatenation averages all the heads' outputs together into a single blended vector
Concatenation discards every head's output except the one with the highest attention scores
explanation: Concatenation is purely a side-by-side placement operation; without the learned output projection W_O afterward, the heads' information would remain unmixed, like separate reports stapled together.

promptText: What is the specific role of the output projection matrix W_O in multi-head attention?
options: It is the only point in the mechanism where information from different heads is actually mixed into a unified representation, via a learned linear combination
It computes the softmax normalization for each individual head's attention weights
It generates the causal mask that is applied identically across all heads
It projects the input embedding into each head's separate Query, Key, and Value vectors
explanation: W_O is applied to the concatenated heads' output and is the sole learned mechanism that blends per-head signals together into one combined representation for the rest of the layer.

promptText: Do different attention heads within the same layer see different subsets of the input tokens?
options: No — every head sees the exact same full sequence and the same masking rules; what differs between heads is only the learned projection matrices applied to that shared input
Yes — each head is assigned a distinct, non-overlapping subset of tokens to reduce total compute
Yes — heads see overlapping but randomly resampled subsets of tokens at every training step
It depends on whether the layer is part of an encoder or a decoder
explanation: Multi-head attention splits the representation dimension across heads, not the input sequence — every head receives the identical full set of tokens and masks, differing only in its independently learned W_Q, W_K, W_V.

promptText: How does the total parameter count of the combined Q/K/V projections across all heads compare to a single full-size attention head, when the standard convention d_k = d_model / num_heads is followed?
options: It stays approximately the same regardless of how many heads are used, because increasing head count proportionally shrinks each head's projection size
It multiplies linearly with the number of heads, since each head needs its own full-size projection matrices
It decreases the more heads are added, because smaller matrices always mean fewer total parameters
It depends only on d_v and is completely unrelated to num_heads or d_k
explanation: Total Q/K/V parameters equal h × d_model × d_k × 3 = h × d_model × (d_model/h) × 3 = 3 × d_model^2, with h canceling out entirely — the head count is independent of the total parameter count.

promptText: Why does splitting d_model across heads, rather than giving each head the full d_model, achieve representational diversity essentially 'for free' in terms of compute budget?
options: Because h heads each projecting d_model down to d_k = d_model/h use, in total, roughly the same number of parameters and FLOPs as one head projecting d_model to d_model — the head count cancels out of the total parameter formula
Because GPUs execute all heads in genuinely zero-cost parallel hardware lanes regardless of their size
Because every head reuses the exact same weight matrix as every other head, so no new parameters are ever needed
Because only the first head actually performs real computation, while the rest simply copy its output
explanation: The parameter-counting derivation shows total Q/K/V parameters equal 3 x d_model^2 independent of head count, which is the precise mathematical basis for the 'diversity for free' claim about multi-head attention.

promptText: What does empirical head-pruning research (e.g. 'Are Sixteen Heads Really Better than One?') reveal about trained multi-head attention layers, and how should that shape an engineer's mental model of head specialization?
options: A substantial fraction of heads can be removed post-training with only modest accuracy loss, showing trained layers are often over-provisioned and specialization is real but uneven — not every head is uniquely necessary or cleanly interpretable
It proves that every head learns a distinct, human-nameable grammatical role with zero redundancy
It shows multi-head attention provides no measurable benefit over single-head attention in any model
It shows that removing any single head always causes catastrophic, unrecoverable accuracy loss
explanation: Pruning studies find genuine, reproducible specialization in some heads alongside significant redundancy in others — the honest synthesis is that trained multi-head layers are over-provisioned, not that every head is essential or that none are interpretable.

promptText: A model's config reports num_attention_heads=32 and num_key_value_heads=8. What attention variant does this describe, and how many query heads share each Key/Value pair?
options: Grouped-Query Attention (GQA); 32/8 = 4 query heads share each Key/Value pair
Full multi-head attention (MHA); every head has its own fully independent Key/Value pair
Multi-Query Attention (MQA); all 32 heads share a single Key/Value pair
This configuration is invalid, since num_key_value_heads must always equal num_attention_heads
explanation: num_key_value_heads less than num_attention_heads (but greater than 1) is the signature of GQA; the group size is num_attention_heads / num_key_value_heads = 32/8 = 4 query heads per shared KV pair.

promptText: Why does GQA reduce KV-cache memory during autoregressive generation compared to full multi-head attention, without changing the number of independent Query projections?
options: The KV-cache stores one Key and Value vector per KV head (not per query head) per token per layer, so reducing the number of distinct KV projections directly shrinks cache size, while each query head still keeps its own Query projection
GQA reduces memory by storing Query vectors at half precision instead of Key and Value vectors
GQA eliminates the KV-cache entirely by recomputing Keys and Values from scratch at every generation step
GQA reduces memory only because it always uses fewer Transformer layers overall
explanation: Cache size scales with the number of KV heads, not query heads, so shrinking num_key_value_heads directly cuts memory traffic while representational diversity in the Query projections is preserved.

promptText: Why do real implementations typically compute one large W_Q of shape (d_model x d_model) plus a reshape into per-head form, instead of storing num_heads separate smaller (d_model x d_k) matrices?
options: The two are mathematically equivalent, but one large matrix multiply is far better utilized by GPU/TPU hardware than many small, independently launched matrix multiplies, reducing kernel-launch and memory-access overhead
Separate smaller matrices would produce a mathematically different, incorrect result compared to a single combined matrix
A single large matrix is required because deep learning frameworks cannot loop over heads at all
The reshape step itself introduces new learnable parameters that directly improve model quality
explanation: Concatenating the per-head matrices column-wise into one big matrix and reshaping after a single matmul is bit-for-bit equivalent to looping over heads, but dramatically more GPU-efficient since it avoids many small, underutilized kernel launches.

promptText: Why does Multi-Query Attention (MQA) tend to degrade quality more than Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) relative to full multi-head attention, even though both reduce KV-cache size?
options: MQA forces every query head, regardless of specialization, to read from a single shared Key/Value projection, creating a bottleneck that limits how differentiated heads' attention behavior can be; GQA only forces sharing within smaller groups, preserving more distinct KV geometries
MQA uses a fundamentally different similarity function (cosine similarity) instead of the dot product used by GQA
MQA removes the softmax normalization step entirely to save compute, while GQA retains it
MQA and GQA have identical effects on quality; they differ only in implementation complexity
explanation: MQA's single shared KV projection is a harder bottleneck than GQA's per-group sharing, so heads that genuinely need distinct Key/Value geometry are more constrained under MQA, which is why GQA is the more common production default when quality matters.

promptText: For BERT-base (d_model=768, num_heads=12), the total attention-block parameter count (Q/K/V projections plus W_O) works out to exactly 4 x d_model^2. What would happen to this total if num_heads were doubled to 24 while d_model stayed fixed?
options: d_k = 768/12 = 64 would become 768/24 = 32, but the total stays unchanged at 4 x d_model^2, because the head count cancels out of the Q/K/V term (h x d_model x d_k = d_model^2 regardless of h) and W_O never depended on h in the first place
The total would double to 8 x d_model^2, since doubling heads doubles the number of independent projection matrices
d_k would need to double to 128 to keep the parameter total constant, which is impossible without increasing d_model
W_O's shape depends directly on num_heads, so doubling heads would double W_O's size independent of d_model
explanation: Because d_k = d_model/h, the h in h x d_model x d_k cancels exactly, leaving d_model^2 regardless of head count; W_O's shape is (d_model x d_model), also independent of h, so the 4 x d_model^2 total is invariant to the head-count change.

promptText: A team converts a 32-head full-MHA checkpoint to 8-group GQA by mean-pooling each group of 4 KV heads' projections, then runs a short continued-training phase. What is the precise source of approximation error introduced, and why does the follow-up training phase help?
options: Mean-pooling collapses potentially distinct KV geometries from the 4 heads in each group into one averaged projection; the error is proportional to how much those heads' original projections actually differed, and continued training lets the remaining trainable weights (Queries, W_O, downstream layers) partially compensate for the discarded distinguishing information
There is no approximation error at all, since averaging matrices is a lossless linear operation
The error comes entirely from reducing the number of Query heads, not from pooling the Key/Value projections
Continued training is needed only to re-randomize the Query projections, which are otherwise left completely unchanged
explanation: The uptraining approach explicitly accepts that averaging heads loses information proportional to how different those heads originally were, and relies on a short continued-training phase to let the rest of the model compensate rather than expecting the pooled checkpoint to be lossless.

promptText: For a model with 40 layers, num_heads=40 (full MHA), d_k=128, sequence length 8192, batch size 1, 16-bit precision, switching to GQA with num_kv_heads=8 changes the KV-cache size by what ratio, and what does this reveal about where the savings actually come from?
options: The KV-cache shrinks to 8/40 = 0.2 (20%) of the original size, because cache size scales with num_kv_heads (not num_query_heads) x seq_len x d_k x layers — the savings come purely from reducing distinct Key/Value projections, not from any change to sequence length or per-head dimension
The KV-cache shrinks by 8/40 only if the sequence length is also reduced proportionally at the same time
The KV-cache size is unaffected by num_kv_heads and depends only on num_query_heads
The KV-cache actually grows under GQA because extra metadata must be stored to track which heads share each group
explanation: KV-cache size is num_layers x num_kv_heads x seq_len x d_k x 2 x bytes_per_element; only num_kv_heads changes from 40 to 8, giving an exact 8/40 = 0.2 ratio, independent of sequence length or d_k, which stay fixed in this comparison.
